{{Short description|Mathematical conjecture}}
{{other uses|Mirror symmetry (disambiguation)}}
{{technical|date=July 2020}}
In mathematics, '''mirror symmetry''' is a conjectural relationship between certain [[Calabi–Yau manifold]]s and a constructed "mirror manifold".  The conjecture allows one to relate the number of [[rational curve]]s on a Calabi-Yau manifold (encoded as [[Gromov–Witten invariant]]s) to integrals from a family of varieties (encoded as [[Period (algebraic geometry)|period integrals]] on a [[variation of Hodge structure]]s). In short, this means there is a relation between the number of genus <math>g</math> [[algebraic curve]]s of degree <math>d</math> on a Calabi-Yau variety <math>X</math> and integrals on a dual variety <math>\check{X}</math>. These relations were original discovered by [[Philip Candelas|Candelas]], [[Xenia de la Ossa|de la Ossa]], Green, and Parkes<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Candelas|first1=Philip|last2=De La Ossa|first2=Xenia C.|last3=Green|first3=Paul S.| last4=Parkes|first4=Linda|date=1991-07-29|title=A pair of Calabi-Yau manifolds as an exactly soluble superconformal theory| journal=Nuclear Physics B|language=en|volume=359|issue=1|pages=21–74|doi=10.1016/0550-3213(91)90292-6| bibcode=1991NuPhB.359...21C|issn=0550-3213}}</ref> in a paper studying a generic [[quintic threefold]] in <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math> as the variety <math>X</math> and a construction<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|last=Auroux|first=Dennis| date=|title=The Quintic 3-fold and Its Mirror|url=https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/mathematics/18-969-topics-in-geometry-mirror-symmetry-spring-2009/lecture-notes/MIT18_969s09_lec06.pdf|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=}}</ref> from the quintic [[Dwork family]] <math>X_\psi</math> giving <math>\check{X} = \tilde{X}_\psi</math>. Shortly after, [[Sheldon Katz]] wrote a summary paper<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Katz|first=Sheldon|date=1993-12-29|title=Rational curves on Calabi-Yau threefolds|eprint=alg-geom/9312009 }}</ref> outlining part of their construction and conjectures what the rigorous mathematical interpretation could be.

== Constructing the mirror of a quintic threefold ==
Originally, the construction of mirror manifolds was discovered through an ad-hoc procedure. Essentially, to a generic [[quintic threefold]] <math>X \subset \mathbb{CP}^4</math> there should be associated a one-parameter family of [[Calabi–Yau manifold|Calabi-Yau]] manifolds <math>X_\psi</math> which has multiple singularities. After [[blowing up]] these [[Singularity (mathematics)|singularities]], they are resolved and a new Calabi-Yau manifold <math>X^\vee</math> was constructed. which had a flipped Hodge diamond. In particular, there are isomorphisms
<math display="block">H^q(X,\Omega_X^p) \cong H^q(X^\vee, \Omega_{X^\vee}^{3-p})</math>
but most importantly, there is an isomorphism
<math display="block">H^1(X,\Omega_X^1) \cong H^1(X^\vee, \Omega_{X^\vee}^{2})</math>
where the string theory (the ''A-model'' of <math>X</math>) for states in <math>H^1(X,\Omega_X^1)</math> is interchanged with the string theory (the ''B-model'' of <math>X^\vee</math>) having states in <math>H^1(X^\vee, \Omega_{X^\vee}^{2})</math>. The string theory in the A-model only depended upon the Kähler or symplectic structure on <math>X</math> while the B-model only depends upon the complex structure on <math>X^\vee</math>. Here we outline the original construction of mirror manifolds, and consider the string-theoretic background and conjecture with the mirror manifolds in a later section of this article.

=== Complex moduli ===
Recall that a generic [[quintic threefold]]<ref name=":3" /><ref>for example, as a set, a Calabi-Yau manifold is the subset of [[complex projective space]]<math>\{[x_0:x_1:x_2:x_3:x_4] \in \mathbb{CP}^4 : x_0^5 + x_1^5 + x_2^5 + x_3^5 + x_4^5 = 0 \}</math></ref> <math>X</math> in <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math> is defined by a [[homogeneous polynomial]] of degree <math>5</math>. This polynomial is equivalently described as a global section of the [[line bundle]] <math>f \in \Gamma(\mathbb{P}^4,\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^4}(5))</math>.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{cite journal|last=Morrison|first=David R.|year=1993 | title=Mirror symmetry and rational curves on quintic threefolds: a guide for mathematicians|journal=J. Amer. Math. Soc. | volume=6|pages=223–247|doi=10.1090/S0894-0347-1993-1179538-2|arxiv=alg-geom/9202004|s2cid=9228037}}</ref> Notice the [[vector space]] of global sections has dimension<math display="block">\dim { \Gamma (\mathbb {P} ^{4},{\mathcal {O}}_{\mathbb {P} ^{4}}(5))} = 126</math> but there are two equivalences of these polynomials. First, polynomials under scaling by the [[algebraic torus]] <math>\mathbb{G}_m</math><ref>Which can be thought of as the <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math>-[[Group action|action]] on <math>\mathbb{C}^5 - \{ 0\}</math> constructing the [[complex projective space]] <math>\mathbb{CP}^4</math></ref> (non-zero scalers of the base field) given equivalent spaces. Second, projective equivalence is given by the [[Automorphism group|automorphism]] group of <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math>, <math>\text{PGL}(5)</math> which is <math>24</math> dimensional. This gives a <math>101</math> dimensional parameter space<math display="block">U_\text{smooth} \subset \mathbb{P}(\Gamma(\mathbb{P}^4,\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^4}(5)))/PGL(5)</math> since <math>126 - 24 - 1 = 101</math>, which can be constructed using [[Geometric invariant theory]]. The set <math>U_{\text{smooth}}</math> corresponds to the equivalence classes of polynomials which define smooth Calabi-Yau quintic threefolds in <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math>, giving a [[moduli space]] of Calabi-Yau quintics.<ref>More generally, such moduli spaces are constructed using projective equivalence of schemes in a fixed projective space on a fixed [[Hilbert scheme]]</ref> Now, using [[Serre duality]] and the fact each Calabi-Yau manifold has trivial [[canonical bundle]] <math>\omega_X</math>, the space of [[Deformation (mathematics)|deformations]] has an isomorphism<math display="block">H^1(X,T_X) \cong H^2(X,\Omega_X)</math> with the <math>(2,1)</math> part of the [[Hodge structure]] on <math>H^3(X)</math>. Using the [[Lefschetz hyperplane theorem]] the only non-trivial cohomology group is <math>H^3(X)</math> since the others are isomorphic to <math>H^i(\mathbb{P}^4)</math>. Using the [[Euler characteristic]] and the [[Euler class]], which is the [[Chern class|top Chern class]], the dimension of this group is <math>204</math>. This is because
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\chi(X) &= -200 \\
&= h^0 + h^2 - h^3 +h^4 + h^6 \\
&= 1 + 1 - \dim H^3(X) + 1 + 1
\end{align}</math>
Using the [[Hodge structure]] we can find the dimensions of each of the components. First, because <math>X</math> is Calabi-Yau, <math>\omega_X \cong \mathcal{O}_X</math> so<math display="block">H^0(X,\Omega_X^3) \cong H^0(X,\mathcal{O}_X) </math> giving the Hodge numbers <math>h^{0,3} = h^{3,0} = 1</math>, hence <math display="block">\dim H^2(X,\Omega_X) = h^{1,2} = 101</math> giving the dimension of the moduli space of Calabi-Yau manifolds. Because of the [[Bogomolev-Tian-Todorov theorem]], all such deformations are unobstructed, so the smooth space <math>U_\text{smooth}</math> is in fact the [[moduli space]] of quintic threefolds. The whole point of this construction is to show how the complex parameters in this moduli space are converted into [[Kähler manifold|Kähler]] parameters of the mirror manifold.

=== Mirror manifold ===
There is a distinguished family of Calabi-Yau manifolds <math>X_\psi</math> called the [[Dwork family]]. It is the [[Proj construction|projective family]]
<math display="block">X_\psi = \text{Proj} \left(
\frac{\mathbb{C}[\psi][x_0,\ldots, x_4]}{(x_0^5 + \cdots + x_4^5 - 5\psi x_0x_1x_2x_3x_4)}
\right)</math>
over the complex plane <math>\text{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[\psi])</math>. Now, notice there is only a single dimension of complex deformations of this family, coming from <math>\psi</math> having varying values. This is important because the Hodge diamond of the mirror manifold <math>\check{X}</math> has <math display="block">\dim H^{2,1}(\check{X}) = 1.</math>The family <math>X_\psi</math> has symmetry group <math display="block">G = \left\{ (a_0,\ldots, a_4) \in (\mathbb{Z}/5)^5 : \sum a_i = 0 \right\}</math> acting by <math display="block">(a_0,\ldots,a_4)\cdot [x_0:\cdots:x_4] = [e^{ a_0\cdot 2\pi i/5}x_0:\cdots : e^{ a_4 \cdot 2\pi i/5}x_4]</math> Notice the projectivity of <math>X_\psi</math> is the reason for the condition <math display="block">\sum_i a_i = 0.</math> The associated quotient variety <math>X_\psi / G</math> has a [[crepant resolution]] given<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> by blowing up the <math>100</math> singularities <math display="block">\check{X} \to X_\psi / G</math> giving a new Calabi-Yau manifold <math>\check{X}</math> with <math>101</math> parameters in <math>H^{1,1}(\check{X})</math>. This is the mirror manifold and has <math>H^3(\check{X}) = 4</math> where each Hodge number is <math>1</math>.

== Ideas from string theory ==
{{See also|Mirror symmetry (string theory)}}
In [[string theory]] there is a class of models called [[non-linear sigma model]]s which study families of maps <math>\phi: \Sigma \to X</math> where <math>\Sigma</math> is a genus <math>g</math> [[algebraic curve]] and <math>X</math> is [[Calabi-Yau]]. These curves <math>\Sigma</math> are called '''world-sheets''' and represent the birth and death of a particle as a closed string. Since a string could split over time into two strings, or more, and eventually these strings will come together and collapse at the end of the lifetime of the particle, an algebraic curve mathematically represents this string lifetime. For simplicity, only genus 0 curves were considered originally, and many of the results popularized in mathematics focused only on this case.

Also, in physics terminology, these theories are <math>(2,2)</math> [[Heterotic string theory|heterotic string theories]] because they have <math>N=2</math> [[supersymmetry]] that comes in a pair, so really there are four supersymmetries. This is important because it implies there is a pair of operators <math display="block">(Q,\overline{Q})</math> acting on the Hilbert space of states, but only defined up to a sign. This ambiguity is what originally suggested to physicists there should exist a pair of Calabi-Yau manifolds which have dual string theories, one's that exchange this ambiguity between one another.

The space <math>X</math> has a complex structure, which is an [[Newlander–Nirenberg theorem|integrable]] [[almost-complex structure]] <math>J \in \text{End}(TX)</math>, and because it is a [[Kähler manifold]] it necessarily has a [[Symplectic geometry|symplectic structure]] <math>\omega</math> called the '''Kähler form''' which can be [[complexified]] to a '''complexified''' '''Kähler form''' <math display="block">\omega^\mathbb{C} = B + i\omega</math> which is a closed <math>(1,1)</math>-form, hence its cohomology class is in <math display="block">[\omega^\mathbb{C}] \in H^1(X,\Omega_X^1) </math> The main idea behind the Mirror Symmetry conjectures is to study the [[Deformation (mathematics)|deformations]], or [[Moduli space|moduli]], of the complex structure <math>J</math> and the complexified symplectic structure <math>\omega^\mathbb{C}</math> in a way that makes these two ''dual'' to each other. In particular, from a physics perspective,<ref name=":4">{{Cite book| last1=Cox | first1 = David A. |author-link1=David A. Cox | last2 = Katz | first2 = Sheldon | title=Mirror symmetry and algebraic geometry|date=1999 | publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=978-0-8218-2127-5|oclc=903477225}}</ref>{{rp|pp=1–2}} the super conformal field theory of a Calabi-Yau manifold <math>X</math> should be equivalent to the dual super conformal field theory of the mirror manifold <math>X^\vee</math>. Here conformal means [[conformal equivalence]] which is the same as an [[equivalence class]] of complex structures on the curve <math>\Sigma</math>.

There are two variants of the non-linear sigma models called the '''A-model''' and the '''B-model''' which consider the pairs <math>(X,\omega^\mathbb{C})</math> and <math>(X,J)</math> and their moduli.<ref name=":1" />{{rp|at=ch 38 pg 729}}

=== A-model ===

==== Correlation functions from String theory ====
Given a Calabi-Yau manifold <math>X</math> with complexified Kähler class <math>[\omega^\mathbb{C}] \in H^1(X,\Omega_X^1) </math> the nonlinear sigma model of the string theory should contain the three [[Generation (particle physics)|generations]] of particles, plus the [[Electromagnetism|electromagnetic]], [[Weak Force|weak]], and [[Strong Force|strong]] forces.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Hamilton|first=M. J. D.|date=2020-07-24|title=The Higgs boson for mathematicians. Lecture notes on gauge theory and symmetry breaking|class=math.DG|eprint=1512.02632}}</ref>{{rp|p=27}} In order to understand how these forces interact, a three-point function called the [[Yukawa coupling]] is introduced which acts as the [[Correlation function (quantum field theory)|correlation function]] for states in <math>H^1(X,\Omega^1_X)</math>. Note this space is the eigenspace of an operator <math>Q</math> on the [[Hilbert space]] of [[Quantum state|states]] for the string theory.<ref name=":4" />{{rp|pp=3–5}} This three point function is "computed" as
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\langle \omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3 \rangle =& \int_X \omega_1\wedge\omega_2\wedge\omega_3
+ \sum_{\beta\neq 0 }n_\beta\int_\beta\omega_1\int_\beta\omega_2\int_\beta\omega_2
\frac{e^{2\pi i \int_\beta \omega^{\mathbb{C}}}}{1 - e^{2\pi i \int_\beta \omega^{\mathbb{C}}}}
\end{align}</math>
using [[Feynman path integral|Feynman path-integral]] techniques where the <math>n_\beta</math> are the naive number of rational curves with homology class <math>\beta \in H_2(X;\mathbb{Z})</math>, and <math>\omega_i \in H^1(X,\Omega_X)</math>. Defining these '''instanton numbers''' <math>n_\beta</math> is the subject matter of [[Gromov–Witten invariant|Gromov–Witten theory]]. Note that in the definition of this correlation function, it only depends on the Kähler class. This inspired some mathematicians to study hypothetical moduli spaces of Kähler structures on a manifold.

==== Mathematical interpretation of A-model correlation functions ====

In the '''A-model''' the corresponding moduli space are the moduli of [[pseudoholomorphic curve]]s<ref>{{Cite book|last=McDuff | first = Dusa|title=J-holomorphic curves and symplectic topology|date=2012|publisher=American Mathematical Society | others=Salamon, D. (Dietmar)|isbn=978-0-8218-8746-2|edition=2nd|location=Providence, R.I.|oclc=794640223}}</ref>{{rp|p=153}}
<math display="block">\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,k}(X,J,\beta) = \{
(u:\Sigma \to X, j, z_1,\ldots, z_k) : u_*[\Sigma] = \beta, \overline{\partial}_Ju = 0 
\}</math>
or the Kontsevich moduli spaces<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kontsevich|first1=M.|author-link1=Maxim Kontsevich|last2=Manin|first2=Yu|author-link2=Yuri Manin|date=1994|title=Gromov-Witten classes, quantum cohomology, and enumerative geometry|url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.cmp/1104270948|journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics|language=en|volume=164|issue=3|pages=525–562|doi=10.1007/BF02101490|arxiv=hep-th/9402147| bibcode=1994CMaPh.164..525K| s2cid=18626455|issn=0010-3616}}</ref>
<math display="block">\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}(X,\beta) = \{u:\Sigma \to X : u \text{ is stable and } u_*([\Sigma]) = \beta \}</math>
These moduli spaces can be equipped with a [[virtual fundamental class]]
<math display="block">[\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,k}(X,J,\beta)]^{virt}</math> or <math display="block">[\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}(X,\beta)]^{virt}</math>
which is represented as the vanishing locus of a section <math>\pi_{Coker}(v)</math> of a sheaf called the Obstruction sheaf <math>\underline{\text{Obs}}</math> over the moduli space. This section comes from the [[differential equation]]<math display="block">\overline{\partial}_J(u) = v</math> which can be viewed as a perturbation of the map <math>u</math>. It can also be viewed as the [[Poincaré duality|Poincaré dual]] of the [[Euler class]] of <math>\underline{\text{Obs}}</math> if it is a [[Vector bundle]].

With the original construction, the A-model considered was on a generic quintic threefold in <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math>.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Mirror symmetry|date=2003|publisher=American Mathematical Society | last1 = Pandharipande | first1 = Rahul |last2 = Hori | first2 = Kentaro |isbn=0-8218-2955-6|location=Providence, RI|oclc=52374327}}</ref>

=== B-model ===

==== Correlation functions from String theory ====
For the same Calabi-Yau manifold <math>X</math> in the A-model subsection, there is a dual superconformal field theory which has states in the eigenspace <math>H^1(X,T_X)</math> of the operator <math>\overline{Q}</math>. Its three-point correlation function is defined as
<math display="block">\langle \theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3 \rangle =
\int_X\Omega \wedge (\nabla_{\theta_1}\nabla_{\theta_2}\nabla_{\theta_3}\Omega)</math>
where <math>\Omega \in H^0(X,\Omega_X^3)</math> is a holomorphic 3-form on <math>X</math> and for an [[infinitesimal]] deformation <math>\theta</math> (since <math>H^1(X,T_X)</math> is the [[tangent space]] of the moduli space of Calabi-Yau manifolds containing <math>X</math>, by the [[Kodaira–Spencer map]] and the [[Bogomolev-Tian-Todorov theorem]]) there is the Gauss-Manin connection <math>\nabla_\theta</math> taking a <math>(p,q)</math> class to a <math>(p+1,q-1)</math> class, hence
<math display="block">\Omega \wedge (\nabla_{\theta_1}\nabla_{\theta_2}\nabla_{\theta_3}\Omega) \in H^3(X,\Omega_X^3)</math>
can be integrated on <math>X</math>. Note that this correlation function only depends on the complex structure of <math>X</math>.

===== Another formulation of Gauss-Manin connection =====
The action of the cohomology classes <math>\theta \in H^1(X,T_X)</math> on the <math>\Omega \in H^0(X,\Omega_X^3)</math> can also be understood as a cohomological variant of the [[interior product]]. Locally, the class <math>\theta</math> corresponds to a [[Čech cocycle]] <math>[\theta_{i}]_{i \in I}</math> for some nice enough cover <math>\{U_i \}_{i \in I}</math> giving a section <math>\theta_i \in T_X(U_i)</math>. Then, the insertion product gives an element <math display="block">\iota_{\theta_i}(\Omega|_{U_i}) \in H^0(U_i,\Omega_X^2|_{U_i})</math> which can be glued back into an element <math>\iota_\theta(\Omega)</math> of <math>H^1(X,\Omega_X^2)</math>. This is because on the overlaps <math display="block">U_i\cap U_j = U_{ij},</math> <math display="block">\theta_{i}|_{ij} = \theta_{j}|_{ij}</math> giving
<math display="block">\begin{align}
(\iota_{\theta_i}\Omega|_{U_{i}})|_{U_{ij}} &= \iota_{
 \theta_i|_{U_{ij}}
} (\Omega|_{U_{ij}}) \\
&= \iota_{
 \theta_j|_{U_{ij}}
} (\Omega|_{U_{ij}}) \\
&= (\iota_{\theta_j}\Omega|_{U_j})|_{U_{ij}}
\end{align}</math>
hence it defines a 1-cocycle. Repeating this process gives a 3-cocycle <math display="block">\iota_{\theta_1}\iota_{\theta_2}\iota_{\theta_3}\Omega \in H^3(X,\mathcal{O}_X)</math> which is equal to <math>\nabla_{\theta_1}\nabla_{\theta_2}\nabla_{\theta_3}\Omega</math>. This is because locally the Gauss-Manin connection acts as the interior product.

==== Mathematical interpretation of B-model correlation functions ====
Mathematically, the '''B-model''' is a [[Variation of Hodge structures|variation of hodge structures]] which was originally given by the construction from the Dwork family.

=== Mirror conjecture ===
Relating these two models of string theory by resolving the ambiguity of sign for the operators <math>(Q,\overline{Q})</math> led physicists to the following conjecture:<ref name=":4" />{{rp|p=22}} for a Calabi-Yau manifold <math>X</math> there should exist a mirror Calabi-Yau manifold <math>X^\vee</math> such that there exists a mirror isomorphism <math display="block">H^1(X,\Omega_X) \cong H^1(X^\vee, T_{X^\vee})</math> giving the compatibility of the associated A-model and B-model. This means given <math>H \in H^1(X,\Omega_X)</math> and <math>\theta \in H^1(X^\vee,T_{X^\vee})</math> such that <math>H \mapsto \theta</math> under the mirror map, there is the equality of correlation functions<math display="block">\langle H,H,H\rangle = \langle \theta,\theta,\theta\rangle</math> 

This equation relates the number of degree <math>d</math> genus <math>0</math> curves on a quintic threefold <math>X</math> in <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math> (so <math>H^{1,1}\cong \mathbb{Z}</math>) to integrals in a variation of Hodge structures. Further, these integrals are actually computable.
